title: Testing II: test-driven development
subtitle: Red, green, refactor, and faking the outside world
goal: Drive new features with tests first, write pytest-style tests, and isolate code from time, randomness and networks with unittest.mock.
outcomes: Follow the red, green, refactor loop to build a feature
Write pytest-style test functions and table-driven cases
Fake time, random numbers and external services with Mock and patch
Explain test coverage and run examples in docstrings with doctest

slides.title: Mission 36: Tests first
slides.body:
Yesterday you wrote tests **after** the code. Today you flip it: **test-driven development** (TDD). Write a failing test, make it pass, clean up, repeat.

Then you learn to fake the outside world (time, randomness, payment APIs) so tests stay fast and reliable.

items: Red: write a test that fails
Green: write just enough code to pass
Refactor: clean up while tests stay green

slides.say: Yesterday you wrote tests after the code. Today we flip the order. In test driven development you write a failing test first, then just enough code to pass it, then clean up. After that, we learn to fake the outside world, like the clock, random numbers and payment APIs, so your tests stay fast and reliable.

slides.title: Why write the test first?
slides.body:
- you design the function from the **caller's** point of view
- you know exactly when you're done: the test is green
- every line of code exists because a test needed it
- tiny steps mean bugs are found seconds after you make them
slides.say: Why write the test first? Because it forces you to design the function from the caller's point of view before you get lost in the details. You know exactly when you are done, because the test goes green. And since you work in tiny steps, a mistake shows up seconds after you make it, while it is still easy to find.

slides.title: pytest: tests as plain functions
slides.body: Most Python teams use **pytest** (`pip install pytest`). Tests are plain functions named `test_...` with plain `assert`. pytest finds them in `test_*.py` files and shows exactly what differed.
slides.say: In industry, most Python teams use a tool called pytest. Tests become plain functions whose names start with test, using the ordinary assert statement. You type pytest in the terminal, it discovers every test file, runs everything and reports what failed and why. We can't install packages on this phone, so next we build a tiny runner that works the same way.

slides.title: Build a tiny pytest
explain: pytest style: a plain function with a plain assert.
Two spaces become two dashes: a bug.
Find every global whose name starts with test_.
Call it; an AssertionError means it failed.
minitest.py, used next, works the same way.
slides.say: Three pytest style tests for a function that turns a blog title into a web address slug. Our runner finds every global name starting with test, calls it, and counts the passes. It is a few lines, but it is the core idea of pytest. And look: the double space test caught a real bug. From now on we import a slightly nicer version of this runner from a file called minitest.

slides.title: TDD step 1: RED
slides.body: Feature: Indian number grouping. After the last 3 digits, commas go every **2** digits: `₹1,23,456`.
slides.expect:
FAIL test_small
FAIL test_thousands
FAIL test_lakhs
FAIL test_crores
0/4 passed
explain: Our tiny runner, from minitest.py.
A stub: just enough to run the tests.
Each test states one behaviour, from simple to hard.
Pass globals() so the runner can find the tests.
slides.say: Our feature: format rupees the Indian way, with commas for thousands, lakhs and crores. Western formatting gives one hundred twenty three thousand, but Indian users expect one lakh, twenty three thousand. We write four tests first, from small amounts to crores, and a stub that returns nothing. Every test fails. That is red, and it proves our tests can actually fail.

slides.title: TDD step 2: GREEN
slides.expect:
PASS test_small
PASS test_thousands
PASS test_lakhs
PASS test_crores
4/4 passed
explain: A special case for small numbers.
Split off the last 3 digits.
Peel pairs of digits off the right of the head.
Join the pairs, then add the tail.
slides.say: Now we write the simplest code that passes. Keep the last three digits as the tail, then peel off pairs of digits from the right of the head. All four tests pass: green. It is not beautiful yet, with a special case and some repetition, and that is fine. Green first, beautiful second.

slides.title: TDD step 3: REFACTOR
slides.body: Improve the design **without changing behaviour**, then re-run the tests.

left.title: Green, but clunky

right.title: Refactored, still green

visual.verdict: Joining groups + [tail] removes the special case. Re-run the tests: still 4/4, so the refactor is safe.

slides.say: Now refactor. Joining the groups together with the tail handles small numbers naturally, so the special case disappears, and we add type hints and a docstring. Then the crucial step: run the tests again. Still four out of four. Tests are what make refactoring safe instead of scary.

slides.title: The TDD loop
slides.q: You just wrote a new test for a feature that doesn't exist yet. What should you do next?
options: Write the whole feature in one go
Run it and watch it fail
slides.why: Seeing it fail proves the test can detect the missing feature. A test that passes before the code exists is testing nothing, or testing the wrong thing.
slides.say: Quick check on the loop. You have just written a test for a feature that does not exist yet. What is the very next step?

slides.title: Fixtures: shared, fresh test data
slides.body: A **fixture** builds the objects a test needs. In pytest, a test simply *asks* for a fixture by naming it as a parameter, and pytest builds a fresh one for each test.

left.title: unittest

right.title: pytest

visual.verdict: pytest sees the parameter named cart, calls the fixture, and passes the result in.

slides.say: Many tests need the same starting objects: a cart, a user, a database connection. In unittest you build them in set up. Pytest uses fixtures instead: a function marked as a fixture builds the object, and any test that names it as a parameter receives a fresh one. Same idea, less ceremony.

slides.title: Mocks: fake the outside world
slides.body: Code that touches the **clock**, **randomness**, the **network** or a **payment API** is slow, flaky or expensive to test. A `Mock` is a stand-in object: it returns what you tell it and records how it was called.

left.title: Real dependency
left.code:
send_otp(phone, code, SmsGateway())
# slow, costs money, needs internet

right.title: Mock in a test
right.code:
send_otp(phone, code, Mock())
# instant, free, fully controlled

visual.verdict: Pass the dependency in, and tests can swap in a mock.

slides.say: Some code talks to the outside world: the clock, random numbers, an SMS gateway, a payment API. Tests against the real thing are slow, flaky, and sometimes cost money. A mock is a stand-in object. You decide what it returns, and afterwards it tells you exactly how it was called. Think of it as a stunt double for the dangerous scenes.

slides.title: Mock: a fake SMS gateway
slides.code:
from unittest.mock import Mock

def send_otp(phone, code, gateway):
    reply = gateway.send(to=phone, text=f"Your OTP is {code}")
    return reply["status"] == "queued"

gateway = Mock()
gateway.send.return_value = {"status": "queued"}

print(send_otp("9876543210", "4821", gateway))
gateway.send.assert_called_once_with(to="9876543210", text="Your OTP is 4821")
print(gateway.send.call_count)
print(gateway.send.call_args.kwargs["to"])
explain: The gateway is passed in: easy to swap in tests.
A Mock accepts any method call.
Decide what send() returns.
Verify the exact call; this raises AssertionError if it differs.
Mocks record every call.
slides.say: Send OTP receives its gateway as a parameter, which is called dependency injection, and it makes testing easy. We pass a mock and tell its send method what to return. After the call, the mock can confirm it was called exactly once with exactly the right phone number and message. No SMS was sent, and no money was spent.

slides.title: patch: control random numbers
slides.code:
import random
from unittest.mock import patch

def roll_bonus():
    roll = random.randint(1, 6)
    return 100 if roll == 6 else 0

with patch("random.randint", return_value=6):
    print(roll_bonus())

with patch("random.randint", return_value=2):
    print(roll_bonus())

print(roll_bonus() in (0, 100))
explain: Looks up random.randint at call time.
Inside this block, random.randint always returns 6.
Now it always returns 2.
Outside: the real randint is back.
slides.say: A dice game pays a bonus on a six. Random results are impossible to test directly, so patch temporarily replaces random dot randint with a mock that returns whatever we choose. Inside the first with block every roll is a six, inside the second it is a two. When the block ends, the real function is restored automatically.

slides.title: patch: freeze the clock
slides.code:
import time
from unittest.mock import patch

def otp_expired(created_at, ttl=300):
    return time.time() - created_at > ttl

with patch("time.time", return_value=1_000_400):
    print(otp_expired(1_000_000))   # 400 seconds old

with patch("time.time", return_value=1_000_200):
    print(otp_expired(1_000_000))   # 200 seconds old
explain: Depends on the real clock: hard to test.
Pretend 'now' is 400 seconds after creation.
And now only 200 seconds after.
slides.say: OTPs expire after five minutes. Without a mock, testing that means waiting five real minutes. With patch, we freeze time dot time at any moment we like. Four hundred seconds after creation the code is expired, two hundred seconds after it is still valid. Both tests run instantly, every time.

slides.title: Predict: what does a Mock remember?
slides.code:
from unittest.mock import Mock

api = Mock()
api.fetch.return_value = {"runs": 287}
data = api.fetch("IND")
print(data["runs"], api.fetch.call_count, api.save.called)
options: AttributeError: Mock object has no attribute 'save'
slides.why: fetch returned what we configured and was called once. A Mock creates any attribute on demand, so api.save exists, but it was never called. That flexibility can hide typos: use Mock(spec=RealClass) in real projects.
slides.say: A mock cricket API returns a score. What is printed: the runs, how many times fetch was called, and whether save was called?

slides.title: Coverage and doctest
slides.body:
**Coverage** measures which lines your tests actually ran. It finds untested code, but 100% coverage doesn't mean bug-free.

**doctest** runs the examples written in your docstrings, so documentation can never go stale.
slides.say: Coverage tools record which lines ran during your tests and report the ones that never did. It is a great way to find untested code, but remember: a line that ran is not the same as a line that was checked. Doctest is a gem in the standard library. It finds examples in your docstrings, runs them, and checks the output, so your documentation can never lie.

slides.title: doctest: examples that run
slides.code:
import doctest

def gst(amount, rate=18):
    """Return the GST on an amount, rounded to paise.

    >>> gst(100)
    18.0
    >>> gst(250, rate=5)
    12.5
    """
    return round(amount * rate / 100, 2)

print(doctest.testmod())
explain: >>> marks code, as typed in the Python shell.
The next line is the expected output.
Run every docstring example in this file.
slides.say: The docstring shows two examples, written exactly as they would look in the Python shell, with three arrows and then the expected result. Doctest mod finds every such example in the file, runs it and compares the output. Two attempted, zero failed. Change the function and forget the docs, and doctest will tell you.

slides.title: Fix the bug: the patch that does nothing
slides.task: This test patches `random.randint` to force a win, but it keeps failing. The patch replaces the name **on the `random` module**, yet `lucky_draw` uses its own imported copy. Fix `lucky_draw` (not the test).
slides.starter:
from random import randint
from unittest.mock import patch

def lucky_draw():
    return "WIN" if randint(1, 100) == 7 else "TRY AGAIN"

def test_seven_wins():
    with patch("random.randint", return_value=7):
        assert lucky_draw() == "WIN", "randint was patched to 7, so expected WIN"

test_seven_wins()
print("test passed")
slides.solution:
import random
from unittest.mock import patch

def lucky_draw():
    return "WIN" if random.randint(1, 100) == 7 else "TRY AGAIN"

def test_seven_wins():
    with patch("random.randint", return_value=7):
        assert lucky_draw() == "WIN", "randint was patched to 7, so expected WIN"

test_seven_wins()
print("test passed")
slides.tests:
import random as _r
from unittest.mock import patch as _p
_r.seed(1)
with _p("random.randint", return_value=7):
    got = lucky_draw()
assert got == "WIN", "With random.randint patched to 7, lucky_draw() should return 'WIN'. Use import random and call random.randint(...) so the patch is seen."
_r.seed(1)
with _p("random.randint", return_value=3):
    got = lucky_draw()
assert got == "TRY AGAIN", "With random.randint patched to 3, lucky_draw() should return 'TRY AGAIN'."
hints: from random import randint copies the function into your file. Patching random.randint later doesn't touch that copy.
Write import random, then call random.randint(1, 100) inside lucky_draw.
slides.say: A classic mocking bug. The test patches random dot randint, but the function imported its own copy of randint before the patch, so it never sees the fake. The rule professionals learn the hard way: patch where the name is looked up. Fix the function so the test passes.

slides.title: TDD: refunds and paise
slides.task:
Product wants two new behaviours, and the tests are already written (they're **red**):

- refunds: `format_inr(-1500)` → `"-₹1,500"`
- floats show paise: `format_inr(1234.5)` → `"₹1,234.50"`

Make them green **without breaking** the old ones. Ints still show no paise.
slides.starter:
from minitest import run_tests

def format_inr(amount):
    digits = str(amount)
    head, tail = digits[:-3], digits[-3:]
    groups = []
    while head:
        groups.insert(0, head[-2:])
        head = head[:-2]
    return "₹" + ",".join(groups + [tail])

def test_lakhs():            # old behaviour: keep it green
    assert format_inr(123456) == "₹1,23,456"

def test_refund():           # new: red
    assert format_inr(-1500) == "-₹1,500"

def test_paise():            # new: red
    assert format_inr(1234.5) == "₹1,234.50"

run_tests(globals())
slides.solution:
from minitest import run_tests

def format_inr(amount):
    sign = "-" if amount < 0 else ""
    amount = abs(amount)
    if isinstance(amount, float):
        rupees, paise = divmod(round(amount * 100), 100)
        suffix = f".{paise:02d}"
    else:
        rupees, suffix = amount, ""
    digits = str(rupees)
    head, tail = digits[:-3], digits[-3:]
    groups = []
    while head:
        groups.insert(0, head[-2:])
        head = head[:-2]
    return sign + "₹" + ",".join(groups + [tail]) + suffix

def test_lakhs():            # old behaviour: keep it green
    assert format_inr(123456) == "₹1,23,456"

def test_refund():           # new: red
    assert format_inr(-1500) == "-₹1,500"

def test_paise():            # new: red
    assert format_inr(1234.5) == "₹1,234.50"

run_tests(globals())
hints: Handle the sign first: sign = "-" if amount < 0 else "", then work with abs(amount).
For floats: rupees, paise = divmod(round(amount * 100), 100), and add f".{paise:02d}" at the end.
Group the digits of rupees exactly as before, then return sign + "₹" + ... + suffix.
slides.say: Your turn to complete a TDD cycle. Product wants refunds shown with a minus sign, and decimal amounts shown with paise. The tests are already written, and they are red. Extend format inr until everything is green, including the old lakhs test. Then try the tricky cases, like ninety nine point nine nine nine.

slides.title: Test randomness with patch
slides.task:
1. Fix `make_otp()` so it always returns **6 digits**, zero-padded (`42` → `"000042"`), using `random.randint(0, 999999)`.
2. Write `test_make_otp_pads_with_zeros()`: patch `random.randint` to return `42` and assert the result is `"000042"`.

The checker runs your test against a broken `make_otp`; it must fail.
slides.starter:
import random
from unittest.mock import patch

def make_otp():
    return str(random.randint(0, 999999))   # TODO: always 6 digits

def test_make_otp_pads_with_zeros():
    pass   # TODO: patch random.randint to return 42, check "000042"

test_make_otp_pads_with_zeros()
print("test ran")
slides.solution:
import random
from unittest.mock import patch

def make_otp():
    return f"{random.randint(0, 999999):06d}"

def test_make_otp_pads_with_zeros():
    with patch("random.randint", return_value=42):
        assert make_otp() == "000042"

test_make_otp_pads_with_zeros()
print("test ran")
slides.tests:
import random as _r
from unittest.mock import patch as _p
with _p("random.randint", return_value=42):
    got = make_otp()
assert got == "000042", f"With randint patched to 42, make_otp() should return '000042', got {got!r}. Pad with f'{{n:06d}}'."
with _p("random.randint", return_value=987654):
    got = make_otp()
assert got == "987654", f"A 6-digit number needs no padding: expected '987654', got {got!r}."
_r.seed(3)
v = make_otp()
assert isinstance(v, str) and len(v) == 6 and v.isdigit(), f"make_otp() should always return a 6-digit string, got {v!r}."
assert "test_make_otp_pads_with_zeros" in globals(), "Keep the test function named test_make_otp_pads_with_zeros."
assert "patch(" in __code__, "Use patch(\"random.randint\", return_value=42) inside your test."
_g = test_make_otp_pads_with_zeros.__globals__
_orig = _g["make_otp"]
_g["make_otp"] = lambda: str(_r.randint(0, 999999))
try:
    _caught = False
    try:
        test_make_otp_pads_with_zeros()
    except AssertionError:
        _caught = True
    assert _caught, "Your test passed even with a make_otp that forgets the zero padding. Patch randint to return 42, then assert make_otp() == '000042'."
finally:
    _g["make_otp"] = _orig
test_make_otp_pads_with_zeros()
hints: Format with zero padding: f"{n:06d}" turns 42 into '000042'.
Inside the test: with patch("random.randint", return_value=42): assert make_otp() == "000042"
slides.say: OTP codes must always be six digits, even when the random number is small, like forty two. Fix make OTP, then write a test that patches random dot randint to forty two and checks the padding. We will run your test against a broken version too, so make sure it really checks the result.

slides.title: What to mock
slides.q: Which one should you usually NOT mock?
options: A paid SMS API your code calls
The current time, for an expiry check
Your own pure function that adds GST
slides.why: Mock the boundaries: network, time, randomness, files, payment providers. Your own pure logic is fast and deterministic, so test it for real; mocking it would test nothing.
slides.say: Last check. Mocks are powerful, but they can be overused. Which of these should you test for real instead of mocking?

slides.title: Mission 36 complete
points: TDD loop: red (a failing test), green (just enough code), refactor (tests stay green)
pytest style: plain test_ functions with plain assert; fixtures provide fresh test data
Mock objects return what you choose and record how they were called
patch swaps time, random or network calls during a with block; patch where the name is looked up
Coverage shows untested lines; doctest keeps docstring examples honest
slides.say: Mission thirty six complete. You can build features test first, write pytest style tests, and fake the clock, randomness and external services with mocks. Tomorrow we hunt bugs systematically, and replace print statements with proper logging. See you on day thirty seven.
